submission.natural_language_explanation: The pole fires retrospectively on the token that completes a conventional time reference used as a clause-level time adjunct: the '.m' piece of an a.m./p.m. clock time ('The shop shuts at 5 p.m.', 'open from 9 a.m. to 5 p.m.'), a weekday or schedule word that fixes a recurring time or a deadline ('on weekdays', 'Tuesday through Sunday', 'by Friday'), or a period word inside an explicit comparison ('compared with last month', 'than the previous quarter'). It is not a fixed-collocation or number+unit detector: the same time word stays near baseline in attributive use ('the 6 p.m. train was cancelled', 'the 11 a.m. train'), as do vague time words ('noon', 'later'), bare durations that are the object of a verb ('lasted 45 minutes'), full numeric dates ('on 12 June 2019') and non-temporal measures ('weighed 3 kg', '1200 metres long').

adversarial_test_results.prompt:
The Ashfield Community Transport Partnership was formed by a group of residents who were frustrated by the withdrawal of the old county bus service. At the time, people living in the outlying hamlets had no practical way of reaching the town centre without a car, and the nearest hospital was more than twelve miles away. The founders began with two second-hand minibuses, a volunteer rota and a small grant from the parish council, and they spent the first winter working out which journeys people actually needed. Drivers kept notebooks, passengers were interviewed at the village hall, and the routes were redrawn several times before anything resembling a timetable emerged.

Over the following decade the partnership grew into a small charitable company with a fleet of eight vehicles, a workshop and a staff of four part-time coordinators. It took over the dial-a-ride scheme from the district council and began carrying passengers to health appointments, adult education classes and the town market. Funding remained precarious: the partnership relied on a patchwork of grants, fares and donations, and every budget round brought fresh anxiety about whether the service could continue. Volunteers covered the gaps, often driving two or three shifts in a row when a paid driver was ill.

The old depot on Canal Street was eventually replaced by a purpose-built base on the edge of the industrial estate. The new building has room for the buses, a small office, a training room and a bay where mechanics can work under cover. Solar panels on the roof supply most of the electricity, and rainwater is collected for washing the vehicles. The move allowed the partnership to consolidate its workshop and to offer apprenticeships to local school leavers, two of whom have since become full-time drivers.

Coordination is still the hardest part of the job. Each route has to be matched to the needs of the people who use it, and a change to one journey can ripple through the whole network. The coordinators spend much of their time on the telephone, rearranging bookings and reassuring passengers who depend on the service for their only contact with the outside world. A missed connection is not an inconvenience for these passengers; it can mean a missed appointment, a wasted morning, or a day spent waiting at home.

The partnership has also become a social lifeline. Drivers know their regular passengers by name, and the buses are often the only place where some older residents see a friendly face. Some of them have been travelling with the same driver for well over a decade, and they telephone the office as much to chat as to book a seat. The coordinators organise an outing to the coast, a lunch in the village hall and a summer picnic that has grown steadily larger each time it has been held.

Looking ahead, the board hopes to electrify the fleet and to extend the network to two neighbouring parishes that have asked to join. A feasibility study is under way, and the results are expected to be presented to the trustees at their next meeting. The board has also begun talks with the primary school about a walking bus scheme for children who live too far from the village to walk safely on their own. In the meantime, the service continues much as it always has, shaped by the patience of its volunteers and the loyalty of its passengers. Shuttle buses run every twenty minutes on weekdays; the vehicles are reserved for private hire at all other times.
